newsitem.title: UK: German bunds gain supremacy as T-notes cower.
newsitem.headline: German bunds gain supremacy as T-notes cower.

text.p: German Bunds are set to outstrip U.S. Treasuries in the coming weeks as speculation grows that the Federal Reserve will soon step on the monetary brakes to slow the U.S. economy, analysts said on Wednesday.
But the gains for Bund investors may be slim, with yield spread outperformance likely to reach its short-term limit in the 85 to 90 basis points area.
"If anything, there is more scope for the spread to widen with Treasuries underperforming," said Mark Cliffe, international economist at HSBC Markets in London.
The 10-year T-note/Bund spread is currently 76 basis points.
A senior Fed official said on Tuesday the consensus at the central bank was for a 25 basis point rise in the 5.25 percent federal funds rate at its September 24 policy-setting meeting.
The official, speaking anonymously, also told Reuters eight of the 12 regional banks in the Fed system were calling for a 50 basis point hike in the discount rate -- currently 5.0 percent.

The comments bashed U.S. T-bonds, which tumbled a full point as the realisation dawned that subdued inflation data last week were not enough to lure the Fed away from its apparently growing attraction to tighter monetary policy.

"Bunds should certainly be outperforming against this background. We could see the yield spread going to 80 or 90 level easily," said Nigel Richardson, bond economist at Yamaichi International in London.
But analysts said the key to which of the two big hitting debt markets would win out in the medium to long term would be the way the Fed chracterised any future rate rise.
"If they chose to charaterise it as a one-off move then its possible that any immediate sell-off could be reversed in the follwing few weeks," said HSBC's Cliffe.

Some said the market was even prepared to take on two moderate rate tightenings -- one of 25 basis points at the September Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting and another after November presidential elections -- without running too scared.
"A rate hike is needed," said Graham McDevitt, senior analyst at Paribas Capital Markets in London. "But we would say that one or two rate hikes will be enough to slow the economy down sufficiently."
While McDevitt said current market momentum was in favour of Bunds, he said further outperformance in the German market should be viewed with some scepticism.
"We recognise the spread could push out further in the very short term," he said.
"But strategically we believe people should be beginning to take advantage of sell-offs in Treasuries."
But others were not convinced the U.S. market was robust enough to take two interest rate blows without flinching.

"I should imagine that a 25 basis point tightening is priced into the market now, but the only question is whether a 50 basis points hike is priced in -- and that is definitely not the case," Richardson said.
Both Cliffe and Richardson said the risk for investors was that a September rate rise would be seen as the first in a series -- leaving little for T-bonds to crow about.
In 1994, the U.S. market was knocked off its feet after the Fed began a series of aggressive rate rises. Treasuries endured a nine-month bear run.
